meta.location: Zarahemla, the east seashore cities, and the land Bountiful
principles: A vote that settles a dispute and does not end it

world_behind.title: The quarrel starts over particular points of law
world_behind.text: Verse 2 says a part of the people wanted a few points altered, and verse 3 says Pahoran refused. Mormon never says which points.

world_behind.title: Both sides get names
world_behind.text: Verse 5 names the king-men, verse 6 the freemen. Mormon defines each by what it wanted rather than by who led it.

world_behind.title: The vote settles it
world_behind.text: Verse 7 has the voice of the people decide for the freemen. Mosiah 29 had set up exactly this mechanism, and it works.

world_behind.title: The losers refuse to serve
world_behind.text: Verse 13 says the king-men were glad the Lamanites were coming and would not take up arms, because they were angry at the chief judge and the people of liberty.

world_behind.title: Moroni asks for authority before using force
world_behind.text: Verse 15 has him send a petition with the voice of the people, and verse 16 says it was granted. The killing in verse 18 follows a grant.

world_behind.title: Amalickiah's oath is flagged as rash
world_behind.text: Verse 9 has him swear to drink Moroni's blood, and verse 10 says the promise was rash before the chapter shows why.

world_behind.title: The Lamanites take six cities
world_behind.text: Verses 22 through 26 list Moroni, Nephihah, Lehi, Morianton, Omner, Gid, and Mulek. The internal dispute cost the coastline.

words.text: Those who wanted a king. The compound occurs eleven times in this record and never in the King James Bible, and Alma 60 and 62 return to it. Mormon defines them by their aim: to alter the law and overthrow the free government.

Those who wanted the free government kept. The word occurs seven times in this record and never in the King James Bible. Mormon says they had sworn to maintain their rights and their religion by a free government.

Hasty, spoken without weighing it. The word occurs once in this record and twice in the King James Bible, where Ecclesiastes warns against being rash with the mouth before God. Mormon applies it to Amalickiah's oath and lets the chapter prove him right.

High birth, and the claim that goes with it. The word occurs three times in this record and never in the King James Bible, all in this chapter. Verse 21 says those who professed the blood of nobility were brought down to humble themselves like their brethren.

A name or designation. The word occurs once in scripture. Mormon uses it to say that afterward nobody was known by the name king-men, which makes the suppression a matter of the label as well as the faction.
A light throwing spear. The record uses it three times and the King James Bible seven, five of them of Saul throwing one at David. Teancum uses it at close range on a sleeping man.

phrases.term: A few particular points of the law should be altered
phrases.text: Mormon describes the demand and withholds its content. The reader never learns which points, only that Pahoran would not move and that the refusal produced a party.

phrases.term: Those who were desirous that Pahoran should be dethroned from the judgment-seat were called king-men
phrases.text: The name is given with the aim attached. Mormon names the faction in the same sentence that says they wanted a king established over the land.

phrases.term: This matter of their contention was settled by the voice of the people
phrases.text: The mechanism from Mosiah 29 doing its work. The vote goes to the freemen, Pahoran keeps the seat, and the king-men are put to silence.

phrases.term: This was a critical time for such contentions to be among the people of Nephi
phrases.text: Mormon states the timing problem directly. Amalickiah is arming while Zarahemla argues, and the next fifteen verses are the cost of the overlap.

phrases.term: He had sworn to drink the blood of Moroni
phrases.text: An oath recorded so its failure can be recorded. Verse 10 calls it rash, and verse 34 has Amalickiah killed in his sleep by a man he never met in battle.

phrases.term: They were glad in their hearts; and they refused to take up arms
phrases.text: The king-men welcome an invasion. Mormon gives the reason as anger at the chief judge and the people of liberty, which makes the refusal a continuation of the vote by other means.

phrases.term: Give him power to compel those dissenters to defend their country or to put them to death
phrases.text: Moroni asks for the authority in writing, with the voice of the people behind it. The record is careful to show the request before the action.

phrases.term: To pull down their pride and their nobility and level them with the earth
phrases.text: The order as given, with an alternative attached: or they should take up arms and support the cause of liberty. Verse 20 says most of them took the second option.

phrases.term: There were four thousand of those dissenters who were hewn down by the sword
phrases.text: The count. Mormon adds that the surviving leaders were imprisoned because there was no time for trials, which marks the irregularity without excusing it.

phrases.term: Were compelled to hoist the title of liberty upon their towers
phrases.text: The banner of Alma 46 raised under compulsion. Mormon records that the sign of a voluntary covenant was flown by men who had a sword at their backs.

phrases.term: Teancum stole privily into the tent of the king, and put a javelin to his heart
phrases.text: The campaign ends in one sentence. Mormon gives no speech, no confrontation, and no comment, and closes the chapter with the days of Amalickiah ended.

verses.label: v. 1–8
verses.title: The two parties
verses.text: The twenty-fifth year begins in peace. Some want points of the law altered; Pahoran refuses; those who want him gone are called king-men and want a king, and those who back him are called freemen. The voice of the people decides for the freemen. Mormon notes the king-men were of high birth and sought power.

verses.label: v. 9–12
verses.title: The timing
verses.text: Amalickiah has stirred the Lamanites again, armed them, and sworn to drink Moroni's blood, which Mormon calls rash. His army is smaller after the losses but still great, and he comes down himself, at the same time the Nephites are settling their dispute.

verses.label: v. 13–16
verses.title: The refusal
verses.text: The king-men are glad the Lamanites are coming and will not take up arms. Moroni is filled with anger at their stubbornness and petitions the governor, with the voice of the people, for power to compel them or put them to death. It is granted.

verses.label: v. 17–21
verses.title: The suppression
verses.text: His army marches on the king-men, kills four thousand who lift weapons, imprisons the surviving leaders without trial for lack of time, and compels the rest to hoist the title of liberty and take up arms. Nobody afterward is called a king-man.

verses.label: v. 22–26
verses.title: The cost
verses.text: While Moroni is putting down the dissension, the Lamanites take the city of Moroni, then Nephihah, Lehi, Morianton, Omner, Gid, and Mulek, all on the east borders by the seashore.

verses.label: v. 27–32
verses.title: Teancum meets them
verses.text: Amalickiah takes many prisoners and much plunder and marches toward Bountiful, where Teancum meets him with men who have been trained in war. The Lamanites are driven back with great loss, and both armies camp for the night.

verses.label: v. 33–37
verses.title: The tent
verses.text: Teancum and his servant go out by night into a camp asleep from the labors and heat of the day. He puts a javelin through the king's heart without waking the servants, returns, wakes his men, and stands ready. The year ends, and so do the days of Amalickiah.

chapter.title: A working vote does not end the quarrel
chapter.text: The voice of the people settles the matter in verse 7, and the losing side sabotages the war effort in verse 13. Mormon shows the mechanism functioning and being outlasted.

chapter.title: The content of the dispute is withheld
chapter.text: A few particular points of the law, never specified. Mormon keeps the reader's attention on what the factions did rather than on who had the better case.

chapter.title: Refusal to serve is treated as an act of war
chapter.text: The king-men do nothing and the coastline falls. The chapter's structure puts the suppression and the loss of six cities side by side.

chapter.title: Moroni gets authority before he uses force
chapter.text: The petition, the voice of the people, the grant, and then the march. Mormon records the sequence carefully in a chapter where four thousand die.

chapter.title: The record notes the irregularity
chapter.text: Leaders imprisoned without trial because there was no time. Mormon states it plainly and does not defend it.

chapter.title: A voluntary banner is raised by compulsion
chapter.text: The title of liberty goes up on the towers of men who were given a choice between it and the sword. Alma 46 had them running to it freely.

chapter.title: The rash oath frames the ending
chapter.text: Amalickiah swears to drink Moroni's blood in verse 9 and dies in verse 34 without ever reaching him. Mormon flags the oath as rash twenty-five verses early.

chapter.title: The chapter ends without commentary
chapter.text: A javelin, a return, a guard set, and the year closed. Mormon gives the death of the book's most capable villain in four verses and adds nothing.

applications.title: Accept the outcome of the vote you took part in
applications.text: The king-men lost and then withheld their help. When a decision goes against you in a process you agreed to, the question is what you do next.

applications.title: Get the authority before you use the power
applications.text: Moroni petitioned in writing with the voice of the people behind him. When you are about to do something drastic and defensible, make sure the authorization exists first.

applications.title: Notice when the timing is the real problem
applications.text: The dispute would have been survivable at another moment. Ask whether your current argument is worth having now, given what else is happening.

applications.title: Weigh an oath before you swear it
applications.text: Amalickiah promised something spectacular and died without doing it. Say what you will actually do, and leave the dramatic version unsaid.

questions.text: What have I refused to alter, and is it principle or stubbornness?
When did a decision go against me, and how did I behave afterward?
Have I ever been quietly glad about trouble that would hurt people I resent?
What am I about to do that I should get permission for?
Where have I skipped a proper process because there was no time?
What have I displayed publicly that I do not hold privately?
What claim about myself would I have to give up to be humbled like my brethren?
